strengths: The paper partially resolves an important open problem in online inverse linear optimization (and contextual recommendation) by establishing a finite regret bound that is polynomial in the dimension d, specifically O(d log d), when action sets are M-convex.

The core technical idea is both clean and insightful: the local exchange optimality condition of M-convex sets (Proposition 2.4) reduces optimal decision-making to pairwise ordering constraints on the objective vector w*, allowing the learner to leverage order simplices and Grünbaum's volume-shrinkage theorem.

The extension to adversarial corruptions is elegant and requires no prior knowledge of the corruption budget C. Because pairwise comparisons induced by uncorrupted actions must define a directed acyclic graph, any cycle immediately certifies corruption, enabling an adaptive restart scheme with an O((C + 1) d log d) regret guarantee.
The paper is very well-written, with transparent proofs, clear motivation, and an informative progression from the O(d^2) warm-up to the O(d log d) refinement and corruption-robust variant.
The Omega(d) lower bound confirms that the upper bound is tight up to an O(log d) factor.
weaknesses: While the paper notes that the center of gravity in Step 3 can be approximated in polynomial time via random walks (e.g., Lovász & Vempala, 2006; Bertsimas & Vempala, 2004), the impact of sampling error/randomization on the overall algorithmic guarantees is only discussed in passing rather than formally analyzed as an end-to-end randomized algorithm.

The corruption model assumes a bounded number of corrupt rounds C rather than general cumulative suboptimality (though the authors openly discuss this limitation and acknowledge extending it as future work).

The contribution is purely theoretical, without numerical experiments or simulations to demonstrate practical performance or compare the O(d^2) topological sort heuristic against the center-of-gravity approach.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental open problem in online inverse linear optimization: whether a finite regret bound polynomial in the dimension d (independent of the time horizon T) is achievable, successfully answering it in the affirmative for M-convex action sets with an O(d log d) bound.

The core conceptual connection between discrete convex analysis (specifically, the local exchange characterization of optimality on M-convex sets) and order-simplex volume shrinkage via Grünbaum's theorem is elegant, novel, and mathematically sound.

The paper provides an insightful pedagogical structure: starting with a simple, computationally efficient O(d^2) warm-up algorithm based on topological sorting, refining it to O(d log d) via center-of-gravity cuts, and concluding with a near-matching Omega(d) lower bound.

The corruption-robust extension achieves an O((C + 1)d log d) regret bound without requiring prior knowledge of the corruption parameter C, leveraging cycle detection on the comparison graph in an intuitive and robust manner.
The manuscript is clearly written, well-organized, and contextualizes its contributions thoroughly within the relevant literature.
weaknesses: The result relies crucially on the action sets being M-convex (or M-natural convex), which restricts the scope to specific combinatorial structures (e.g., matroids, certain integer resource allocations) and leaves the general polyhedral case unresolved.

The O(d log d) algorithm requires computing or approximating the center of gravity of the polytope Pt in Step 3. While polynomial-time via MCMC/random walks, this is computationally demanding in practice compared to the simple O(d^2) topological sorting algorithm.

The corruption model counts the number of corrupted rounds C rather than general cumulative suboptimality (e.g., sum of suboptimality gaps), which is slightly more restrictive than some recent settings in inverse optimization.

The submission is purely theoretical and lacks numerical experiments or simulations demonstrating the empirical performance and computational feasibility of the proposed algorithms on concrete matroid/M-convex instances.

strengths: Partially resolves an important open question in online inverse linear optimization by establishing the first finite regret bound that scales polynomially in the dimension d (specifically, O(d log d)), independent of the time horizon T, under M-convex action sets.
M-convex sets constitute a significant and practically important class of combinatorial structures, subsuming matroids (e.g., spanning trees, uniform matroids) and extensions to integer lattices.

The technical approach is elegant and sound: it establishes a clean synergy between the local exchange optimality characterization of M-convexity and geometric volume shrinkage via Grünbaum's theorem and the Freudenthal triangulation of the unit cube.

The extension to adversarial corruption is neat and intuitive: by monitoring cycles in the directed comparison graph induced by local exchanges, the algorithm detects corruptions adaptively and restarts, achieving an O((C + 1) d log d) regret bound without prior knowledge of C.
The paper is very well-written, structured clearly, and provides tight complementation with an adapted Omega(d) lower bound.
weaknesses: The exact center-of-gravity calculation in the O(d log d) algorithm is #P-hard. While the authors mention using randomized approximation algorithms (Lovász & Vempala, 2006; Bertsimas & Vempala, 2004), the manuscript lacks a formal theorem/proof accounting for the exact approximation tolerances and failure probabilities on the resulting regret bound.
The results rely specifically on the exchange properties of M-convexity, so the question of achieving a polynomial-in-d finite regret bound for general polyhedral action sets remains open.

The paper is entirely theoretical with no empirical simulations illustrating the practical performance, runtime trade-offs (e.g., between the exact O(d^2) topological sort algorithm and the center-of-gravity method), or corruption-detection behavior.

strengths: The paper partially resolves a prominent open question in online inverse linear optimization by establishing the first finite, polynomial-in-d regret bound of O(d log d) when action sets are M-convex.

The technical approach elegantly integrates discrete convex analysis (the exchange property and local optimality conditions on M-convex sets) with classical geometric volume arguments (Grünbaum's theorem and order simplices).
The extension to adversarial corruption achieving O((C + 1) d log d) regret without knowing C is neat, utilizing cycle detection on the comparison graph to trigger restarts.

The paper is very well written, clearly structured, and provides transparent explanations, including a gentle progression from the warm-up O(d^2) algorithm to the optimal O(d log d) algorithm, with rigorous proofs and detailed appendix discussions on polynomial-time approximations.
weaknesses: Under M-convex action sets, the linear optimization problem relies primarily on the relative ordering of the components of w*, effectively reducing the continuous parameter estimation problem to learning a permutation/partial order. While this is an insightful observation, it represents a notable structural simplification compared to general polyhedral action sets.

The O(d log d) algorithm relies on computing the center of gravity of the consistent polytope, which is #P-hard in general; although an approximate center of gravity via random walks runs in polynomial time, the per-round complexity is relatively high (O~(d^6 log d log T)).

The empirical evaluation in Appendix C is minimal and restricted to a small synthetic uniform matroid benchmark (d = 20), though this is acceptable given the primarily theoretical nature of the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant open problem in online inverse linear optimization: obtaining a finite regret bound (independent of the time horizon T) that scales polynomially in the problem dimension d. The authors successfully achieve an O(d log d) bound for the broad and important family of M-convex action sets (subsuming matroids).

The theoretical framework is elegant and coherent. Exploiting the discrete convex analysis property that local exchanges characterize global optimality on M-convex sets reduces the problem of learning w* to discovering pairwise coordinate orderings. Combining this with Grünbaum's theorem and the Freudenthal triangulation (order simplices) yields a sharp volume shrinkage analysis.

The extension to adversarial corruption is well-conceived. Using the acyclicity of the pairwise comparison graph as a corruption certificate enables an adaptive restart mechanism that achieves O((C + 1) d log d) regret without requiring prior knowledge of C.

The manuscript is written with exceptional clarity. The progression from the O(d^2) warm-up algorithm to the O(d log d) refined method, followed by the corruption-robust version and matching lower bound (up to log d), makes the core technical intuition transparent.

The authors provide a thorough analysis of computational complexity, detailing polynomial-time guarantees via hit-and-run sampling (Appendix A and B) and an honest treatment of the tied-component assumption (Appendix D).
weaknesses: The O(d log d) algorithm relies on computing or approximating the center of gravity of the polytope Pt. While polynomial-time via hit-and-run sampling, the per-round computational complexity is roughly O~(d^6 log d log T), which is prohibitive for moderate to large d. In contrast, the simpler O(d^2) topological sort variant runs in O(d^2) per round and exhibits competitive empirical performance in the reported experiment.

The corruption-robustness mechanism relies fundamentally on Assumption 2.2(2) (distinctness of components of w*). As noted in Appendix D, if components are equal, cycles can appear without any corruptions, breaking the simple restart certificate. Overcoming this limitation in the corrupted setting remains an open challenge.
The corruption model counts the number of suboptimal rounds C rather than measuring cumulative metric suboptimality (as explored in some recent literature, e.g., Sakaue et al., 2025b).

strengths: Addresses an important and long-standing open question in online inverse linear optimization: obtaining a finite regret bound that scales polynomially in the dimension d, resolving it for the broad and practically relevant class of M-convex action sets (which subsumes matroids).

The theoretical methodology is novel and elegant: it leverages the local exchange characterization of optimal solutions on M-convex sets (Murota, 2003) together with Grünbaum's theorem on center-of-gravity slicing and the Freudenthal triangulation (order simplices) of the unit cube to establish the O(d log d) finite regret bound.

The extension to adversarial corruption is neat and insightful: by monitoring the acyclicity of the directed graph induced by pairwise inequalities, the algorithm detects corruptions adaptively and achieves an O((C + 1)d log d) regret bound via restarts without needing prior knowledge of C.

The paper is exceptionally well structured and clearly presented. The progression from the warm-up O(d^2) algorithm to the O(d log d) volume-based method, followed by the corruption extension, makes the core intuition easy to follow.
Complements the upper bounds with an Omega(d) lower bound tailored to M-convex action sets via an M-natural-convex embedding, proving that the O(d log d) bound is tight up to a logarithmic factor.
weaknesses: Computing the exact center of gravity is #P-hard. While the paper provides a polynomial-time randomized approximation via hit-and-run sampling in Appendix A, the theoretical per-round runtime is relatively high (O~(d^6 log d log T)), which may limit the scalability of the O(d log d) variant for large dimensions compared to the simpler O(d^2) topological sort algorithm.

The corruption model assumes a bounded number of corrupted rounds C rather than cumulative suboptimality corruption, and the corruption detection crucially relies on the distinctness assumption of w* (as explained in Appendix D), which limits robustness when coordinates of w* are identical.

The empirical evaluation is limited to a small-scale synthetic experiment on uniform matroids (d = 20, five trials); broader simulations across diverse matroid structures (e.g., graphic matroids) would have further illustrated practical behavior.
